metadata.title: Why Two AIs Checking Each Other Is One Blind Spot Twice
metadata.purpose: Show how common cause failure in AI monitoring means a checker trained on the same foundation as the generator shares its blind spots — so the exact error most likely to fool the generator sails through the monitor too. Source: books/computational-skepticism-for-ai/chapters/13-accountability-who-is-responsible-when-the-system-fails.md

props.title: Why Two AIs Checking Each Other Is One Blind Spot Twice

card.copy:
Why Two AIs Checking Each Other
Is One Blind Spot Twice

beats.narration_text: The system design sounds rigorous: an AI generates medical imaging reports. A second AI reviews every report before it reaches the radiologist. Two independent checks. Redundancy. Safety. Then a rare imaging artifact — one that both models were trained on data that systematically underrepresented — slips through. Not because either model was weak. Because both models had the same hole, in the same place, because they were built on the same foundation. Two sieves. Same hole. The grain that would fit through the first sieve is precisely the grain that fits through the second.

What does a checker catch
when it shares the same foundation?

beats.narration_text: Two models trained on the same dataset develop correlated error patterns. Where the data is dense and well-labeled, both models learn well. Where the data is sparse, inconsistently labeled, or structurally biased — both models learn the same deficient representation. The errors are not independent. They are products of the same training distribution. An error that fools Model A is systematically more likely to fool Model B if both were trained on the same data, because both learned from the same gaps.

beats.narration_text: The redundancy intuition assumes independent failures — if Model A fails with probability p, and Model B fails independently with the same probability, the chance of both failing is p squared, which is much smaller than p. That math only works if the failures are independent. When failures are correlated — when both models are more likely to fail on exactly the same inputs — the combined system's failure rate is not p squared. It approaches p. The second check adds operational cost without adding proportional safety.

beats.image_description: Two circular sieves shown side by side at a slight angle — both slate-colored wire mesh — each with a matching crimson hole in exactly the same position, a gold-glowing grain falling from above, passing cleanly through the first sieve's hole and then through the identical hole in the second sieve, disappearing into dark space below while all the teal valid grains are caught on the mesh surfaces — clean, geometric, merciless

beats.narration_text: Here are two sieves. The left sieve is the generator. The right sieve is the checker. Both are made of the same mesh — same training data. Teal grains — valid outputs — hit the mesh and stay caught. Now a crimson hole appears on the left sieve: a class of errors the generator was never trained to recognize. Watch where the hole appears on the right sieve. Same position. Same size. The gold grain — the error that fits the hole — falls through the left sieve. It approaches the right sieve. It fits the hole there too. Both sieves. Same gap. The grain is through.

beats.narration_text: This is the common cause failure mode from reliability engineering — when multiple independent-seeming components share a common failure cause, redundancy provides less protection than the independence assumption suggests. In aviation and nuclear engineering, this is why redundant systems must use different physical principles, different manufacturers, and different design teams. The redundancy must be genuine independence, not duplicated architecture. Two GPT-4 calls are not two independent checks. They are one check, twice.

beats.narration_text: For AI system design, a checker must come from outside the shared foundation to provide genuine independence. This can mean: a model trained on different data sources; a model using a different architecture; a deterministic rule-based system; a statistical audit tool; or a human reviewer. The check's independence must be established relative to the generator's failure modes — not just relative to its architecture. Different architecture, same training data — still correlated. Same architecture, different data — also correlated, differently.

beats.narration_text: The dangerous variant of this failure is when the monitoring system was explicitly trained to verify the generator's outputs. A verifier trained on examples of correct and incorrect generator outputs learns the generator's pattern of errors — including what a plausible-sounding but wrong output looks like in the generator's style. The verifier can become very good at catching the errors it was trained on, while remaining blind to the errors the generator produces that were not in the verifier's training set.

beats.narration_text: The design question to ask before adding an AI checker is: what is the failure mode that most concerns me in the generator, and does the proposed checker have genuine independence from that failure mode? If the answer is 'the checker was trained on the same data,' the independence is not genuine for failures that originate in that data. The checker adds a performance layer. It does not add a safety layer against the same-foundation failures. Document which failures the checker genuinely catches and which it does not.

beats.narration_text: A financial institution deploys a loan underwriting AI, then adds a second AI to flag cases the first model may have mishandled — a compliance monitor. Both are fine-tuned versions of the same foundation model on the institution's historical loan data. A regulatory audit identifies a pattern: the monitoring AI is catching formatting errors, policy-rule violations, and obvious outliers — things the base model handles badly regardless of fine-tuning. But a category of borderline fair-lending cases — applicants near the margin in demographics that were underrepresented in the training data — is being passed by both models at the same rate as their individual pass rates. The monitor is not providing independent coverage of the exact failure type the regulator cares about most, because the failure type is a product of the shared training gap. The institution reports that the system has dual-AI review. The regulator asks for the independence analysis. There is none.

beats.narration_text: A checker trained on the same foundation as the generator shares its blind spots — this is common cause failure: the error most likely to fool the generator is precisely the error most likely to pass through the monitor, so two correlated systems fail together rather than catching each other. Real independence requires the checker to come from outside the shared failure cause — different data sources, different methods, or a human reviewer — and that independence must be verified for the specific failure modes that matter most.
